claim: Human perception of contrast is stable even when the visual environment is quickly changing.
source: Yet, human perception of contrast is stable even when the visual environment is quickly changing, suggesting rapid post receptor luminance gain control.
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on human visual perception

claim: In Drosophila, luminance gain control leads to luminance invariant behavior for moving OFF stimuli.
source: Similarly, in the fruit fly Drosophila, such gain control leads to luminance invariant behavior for moving OFF stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ketkar et al., 2020)

claim: Behavioral responses to moving ON stimuli utilize a luminance gain.
source: Here, we show that behavioral responses to moving ON stimuli also utilize a luminance gain, and that ON-motion guided behavior depends on inputs from three first-order interneurons L1, L2, and L3.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: ON-motion guided behavior depends on inputs from three first-order interneurons L1, L2, and L3.
source: Here, we show that behavioral responses to moving ON stimuli also utilize a luminance gain, and that ON-motion guided behavior depends on inputs from three first-order interneurons L1, L2, and L3.
evidence: Supported by behavioral silencing and rescue experiments

claim: Each of L1, L2, and L3 neurons encodes contrast and luminance differently.
source: Each of these neurons encodes contrast and luminance differently and distributes information asymmetrically across both ON and OFF contrast-selective pathways.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing distinct response properties

claim: L1, L2, and L3 distribute information asymmetrically across both ON and OFF contrast-selective pathways.
source: Each of these neurons encodes contrast and luminance differently and distributes information asymmetrically across both ON and OFF contrast-selective pathways.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments showing contributions to both pathways

claim: Behavioral responses to both ON and OFF stimuli rely on a luminance-based correction provided by L1 and L3.
source: Behavioral responses to both ON and OFF stimuli rely on a luminance-based correction provided by L1 and L3, wherein L1 supports contrast computation linearly, and L3 non-linearly amplifies dim stimuli.
evidence: Supported by silencing and rescue experiments showing luminance-dependent effects

claim: L1 supports contrast computation linearly.
source: Behavioral responses to both ON and OFF stimuli rely on a luminance-based correction provided by L1 and L3, wherein L1 supports contrast computation linearly, and L3 non-linearly amplifies dim stimuli.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing linear luminance scaling in L1

claim: L3 non-linearly amplifies dim stimuli.
source: Behavioral responses to both ON and OFF stimuli rely on a luminance-based correction provided by L1 and L3, wherein L1 supports contrast computation linearly, and L3 non-linearly amplifies dim stimuli.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing non-linear luminance responses in L3

claim: Contrast encoding in photoreceptors is not luminance invariant when the stimulus changes more rapidly than photoreceptor adaptation.
source: However, contrast encoding in photoreceptors is not luminance invariant when the stimulus changes more rapidly than photoreceptor adaptation (Laughlin and Hardie, 1978; Normann and Werblin, 1974), arguing for a common post-receptor corrective mechanism.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on photoreceptor physiology

claim: Information is split into two separate ON and OFF pathways in most visual systems.
source: In most visual systems, information is split into two separate ON and OFF pathways, that process contrast increments (ON) or contrast decrements (OFF), respectively (Behnia et al., 2014; Franceschini et al., 1989; Silies et al., 2014; Yang and Clandinin, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on visual system organization

claim: The visual OFF pathway in fruit flies drives luminance-invariant behavior.
source: The visual OFF pathway in fruit flies drives luminance-invariant behavior (Ketkar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Luminance serves as a corrective signal in the OFF pathway, leading to a luminance gain that adjusts temporal contrast computation when background luminance quickly changes.
source: Luminance serves as a corrective signal, leading to a luminance gain that adjusts temporal contrast computation when background luminance quickly changes (Ketkar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: ON and OFF pathways are not mere sign-inverted versions of each other.
source: However, the ON and OFF pathways are not mere sign-inverted versions of each other since they face different environmental challenges (Clark et al., 2014; Ruderman and Bialek, 1994) and have evolved several structural and physiological asymmetries (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Jin et al., 2011; Leonhardt et al., 2016; Ratliff et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on pathway asymmetries

claim: ON and OFF contrast selectivity first arises two synapses downstream of photoreceptors, in medulla neurons.
source: ON and OFF contrast selectivity first arises two synapses downstream of photoreceptors, in medulla neurons (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Serbe et al., 2016; Silies et al., 2013; Strother et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on Drosophila visual system

claim: L1 is thought to be the sole major input of the ON pathway.
source: L1 is thus thought to be the sole major input of the ON pathway, whereas L2 and L3 are considered the two major inputs of the OFF pathway (Figure 1A; Clark et al., 2011; Joesch et al., 2010; Shinomiya et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature, but challenged by current study

claim: L2 and L3 are considered the two major inputs of the OFF pathway.
source: L1 is thus thought to be the sole major input of the ON pathway, whereas L2 and L3 are considered the two major inputs of the OFF pathway (Figure 1A; Clark et al., 2011; Joesch et al., 2010; Shinomiya et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: L2 is contrast sensitive but cannot support luminance invariance alone when photoreceptor adaptation is insufficient.
source: Among these, L2 is contrast sensitive, but cannot support luminance invariance alone when photoreceptor adaptation is insufficient.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ketkar et al., 2020)

claim: The stable computation of contrast at changing background luminance in OFF-motion guided behavior is ensured by a corrective signal from luminance-sensitive L3 neurons.
source: Instead, the stable computation of contrast at changing background luminance in OFF-motion guided behavior (OFF behavior) is ensured by a corrective signal from luminance-sensitive L3 neurons (Ketkar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Fly turning responses to moving ON edges were similar across luminances, with low-luminance edges eliciting slightly larger turning responses than brighter edges.
source: Fly turning responses were similar across luminances, with low-luminance edges eliciting slightly larger turning responses than brighter edges (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C

claim: L1 responded negatively to contrast increments.
source: As described previously, L1 responded negatively to contrast increments, in line with the inverted response polarity of lamina neurons (Figure 1D; Clark et al., 2011; Laughlin and Hardie, 1978; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1D and citations to previous work

claim: The absolute response amplitude of L1 calcium signals scaled with luminance, showing smaller response in low as compared to high luminances.
source: The absolute response amplitude of the L1 calcium signals scaled with luminance, showing smaller response in low as compared to high luminances, and did not co-vary with the behavioral response (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1E

claim: L1 signals and behavioral responses had opposite luminance dependencies.
source: L1 signals and behavioral responses had opposite luminance dependencies (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 1E

claim: L1 and L2 showed transient negative responses when luminance stepped up, and transient-positive responses when luminance stepped down.
source: L1 and L2 showed transient negative responses when luminance stepped up, and transient-positive responses when luminance stepped down (Figure 2A), consistent with the contrast sensitivity described for L1 and L2 (Clark et al., 2011; Silies et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2A and citations to previous work

claim: L2 did not show any sustained component.
source: L2 did not show any sustained component.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2A

claim: L3 showed sustained responses to OFF steps and was non-linearly tuned to stimulus luminance, responding strongly to the darkest stimulus.
source: L3 showed sustained responses to OFF steps and was non-linearly tuned to stimulus luminance, responding strongly to the darkest stimulus.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2A

claim: L1 showed a transient component followed by a sustained component, suggesting that it encodes luminance in addition to contrast.
source: Intriguingly, L1 showed a transient component followed by a sustained component, suggesting that it encodes luminance in addition to contrast (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2A

claim: The sustained components of L1 responses were negatively correlated with luminance, such that the baseline calcium signal at each step sequentially increased with decreasing stimulus luminance.
source: The sustained components of L1 responses were negatively correlated with luminance, such that the baseline calcium signal at each step sequentially increased with decreasing stimulus luminance.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2A

claim: The transient peak responses of L1 neurons correlated positively with the A step contrast and were indistinguishable for the B steps.
source: The transient peak responses of L1 neurons correlated positively with the A step contrast and were indistinguishable for the B steps.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: L1, like L2, encodes contrast in its peak response.
source: This suggests that L1, like L2, encodes contrast in its peak response (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, tested with one-way ANOVA), (Ketkar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data and statistical testing

claim: The sustained component of L1 responses negatively correlated with the luminance values of both A and B steps, indicating luminance encoding.
source: The sustained component of L1 responses negatively correlated with the luminance values of both A and B steps, indicating luminance encoding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C

claim: L1 neurons encode contrast in their peak responses and luminance in their sustained responses.
source: Together, L1 neurons encode contrast in their peak responses and luminance in their sustained responses.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing distinct response components

claim: L1 and L2 responded similarly to low-contrast stimuli, but L2 responses tended to be higher for high contrasts.
source: Although L1 and L2 responded similarly to low-contrast stimuli, L2 responses tended to be higher for high contrasts (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2B

claim: L1 neuron contrast functions had steeper slopes and thus, L1 reached saturation at lower contrasts than L2.
source: L1 neuron contrast functions had steeper slopes and thus, L1 reached saturation at lower contrasts than L2, suggesting that L1 neurons encode contrasts with less resolution than L2 neurons do, especially in the high-contrast regimes.
evidence: Supported by sigmoidal fitting analysis of calcium imaging data

claim: L1 neurons dedicated less response range to encode contrast than L2 neurons.
source: Furthermore, analysis of the scaling parameter revealed that L1 neurons dedicated less response range to encode contrast than L2 neurons (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sigmoidal fit parameters in Figure 2C and D

claim: L2 transient responses returned to baseline within the 10 s of the stimulus presentation, whereas both L1 and L3 displayed sustained components that varied with luminance.
source: As for the staircase stimulus, L2 transient responses returned to baseline within the 10 s of the stimulus presentation, whereas both L1 and L3 displayed sustained components that varied with luminance (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2E and F

claim: Sustained response components in L1 and L3 carried similar mutual information with luminance, and both were higher than L2.
source: Sustained response components in L1 and L3 carried similar mutual information with luminance, and both were higher than L2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by mutual information analysis in Figure 2G

claim: L1 responses were more linear with respect to luminance than L3 responses, which selectively amplified low luminance.
source: L1 responses were more linear with respect to luminance than L3 responses, which selectively amplified low luminance (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by non-linearity analysis in Figure 2H

claim: L1 silencing had little effect on responses to 100% contrast at varying luminance.
source: L1 silencing had little effect on responses to 100% contrast at varying luminance, suggesting the existence of other ON-pathway inputs (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3A and B

claim: L1 silenced flies turned normally to ON edges of fixed luminance.
source: L1 silenced flies also turned normally to ON edges of fixed luminance, ruling out the possibility that changing luminance underlies this inconsistency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: L1 silencing severely reduced turning responses when a bright instead of a dark inter-stimulus interval was used.
source: However, L1 silencing severely reduced turning responses when a bright instead of a dark inter-stimulus interval was used, explaining the discrepancy between this and previous studies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D

claim: L1 is a major but not the sole input to the ON pathway.
source: Thus, L1 is indeed a major but not the sole input to the ON pathway.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral silencing experiments showing partial effects

claim: Flies in which ort expression was rescued in L1 responded to ON motion at all luminances, and indistinguishable from controls.
source: Flies in which ort expression was rescued in L1 responded to ON motion at all luminances, and indistinguishable from controls (Figure 3F), showing that L1 can mediate normal turning behavior to ON edges at all luminances.
evidence: Supported by behavioral rescue data in Figure 3F

claim: L1 can mediate normal turning behavior to ON edges at all luminances.
source: Flies in which ort expression was rescued in L1 responded to ON motion at all luminances, and indistinguishable from controls (Figure 3F), showing that L1 can mediate normal turning behavior to ON edges at all luminances.
evidence: Supported by behavioral rescue data in Figure 3F

claim: L3-silenced flies responded stronger to all ON edges compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, unlike controls, L3-silenced flies responded stronger to all ON edges, revealing a potential, unexplored role of L3 in inhibiting behavioral responses to certain stimuli.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4A and B

claim: L3 silenced flies did not show a slight increase in turning amplitude at lower edge luminance, unlike controls.
source: However, the responses of L3-silenced flies were still similar across luminances (Figure 4A and B). Unlike controls, L3 silenced flies did not show a slight increase in turning amplitude at lower edge luminance, also reflected in the differences in their slopes (Figure 4C), suggesting that L3 inputs to the ON pathway also contribute to behavior in a luminance-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4A, B, and C

claim: L3 ort rescue flies turned to ON edges at all luminances tested.
source: L3 ort rescue flies turned to ON edges at all luminances tested (Figure 4D) and significantly rescued turning behavior at low luminances compared to ort mutant flies (Figure 4E), showing that L3 is sufficient for ON behavior at low luminances.
evidence: Supported by behavioral rescue data in Figure 4D and E

claim: L3 is sufficient for ON behavior at low luminances.
source: L3 ort rescue flies turned to ON edges at all luminances tested (Figure 4D) and significantly rescued turning behavior at low luminances compared to ort mutant flies (Figure 4E), showing that L3 is sufficient for ON behavior at low luminances.
evidence: Supported by behavioral rescue data in Figure 4D and E

claim: Flies lacking both L1 and L3 functional outputs still turned to moving ON edges.
source: Flies still turned to the moving ON edges. However, unlike control responses which slightly deviated from luminance invariance by showing a negative correlation with luminance, turning responses of flies lacking both L1 and L3 functional outputs were positively correlated with luminance (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4F–H

claim: Behavioral responses of flies lacking both L1 and L3 underestimated dim stimuli.
source: Intriguingly, behavioral responses of flies lacking both lamina neurons carrying luminance information underestimated dim stimuli (Figure 4G), and qualitatively recapitulated the LMC contrast-sensitive responses (Ketkar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4G

claim: L1 and L3 can together account for the luminance information available to the ON pathway.
source: Thus, L1 and L3 can together account for the luminance information available to the ON pathway.
evidence: Inferred from double silencing experiments showing luminance-dependent deficits

claim: L1 fully rescued turning behavior to ON edges at all luminances.
source: Whereas L1 fully rescued turning behavior to ON edges at all luminances, L3 significantly rescued turning behavior selectively at low luminances (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by rescue efficiency analysis in Figure 4I

claim: L3 significantly rescued turning behavior selectively at low luminances.
source: Whereas L1 fully rescued turning behavior to ON edges at all luminances, L3 significantly rescued turning behavior selectively at low luminances (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by rescue efficiency analysis in Figure 4I

claim: L3 is a functional input to the ON pathway.
source: Taken together, L3 is a functional input to the ON pathway, to which L1 and L3 both provide distinct types of luminance information (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by behavioral silencing and rescue experiments

claim: Flies lacking both L1 and L3 still respond to moving ON edges, suggesting the existence of an unidentified contrast input.
source: Because flies lacking both neurons still respond to moving ON edges, our data suggest the existence of an unidentified contrast input.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data showing residual responses

claim: L2-silenced flies showed only slightly reduced turning to all ON edges as compared to controls.
source: L2-silenced flies showed only slightly reduced turning to all ON edges as compared to controls (Figure 5A and B) similarly to silencing L1 alone (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A and B

claim: When L1 and L2 were silenced together, fly turning responses were fully disrupted across conditions.
source: However, when L1 and L2 were silenced together, fly turning responses were fully disrupted across conditions (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5C and D

claim: L2, together with L1, is required for ON behavioral responses across different contrasts and luminances.
source: This shows that L2, together with L1, is required for ON behavioral responses across different contrasts and luminances.
evidence: Supported by double silencing experiments showing complete loss of responses

claim: L1, L2, and L3 are all ON-pathway inputs.
source: Altogether, L1, L2, and L3 are all ON-pathway inputs.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral experiments showing contributions of all three neurons

claim: When L1 was silenced, behavioral responses to OFF edges were no longer invariant across luminance.
source: Similarly, when L1 was silenced, behavioral responses were no longer invariant across luminance, but flies turned less to –100% contrast at low luminance as compared to high luminance (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 6A and B

claim: L1 inputs provide a luminance gain to the OFF pathway.
source: These data demonstrate that L1 inputs provide a luminance gain to the OFF pathway.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral silencing experiments showing luminance-dependent deficits

claim: L1 ort rescue flies responded similarly to positive controls at low luminances, rescuing responses to OFF edges at dim backgrounds.
source: L1 ort rescue flies responded similarly to positive controls at low luminances, rescuing responses to OFF edges at dim backgrounds (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral rescue data in Figure 6C and D

claim: L1 is sufficient to guide OFF behavior under the same conditions that were previously described for L3.
source: Therefore, L1 is even sufficient to guide OFF behavior under the same conditions that were previously described for L3 (Ketkar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by behavioral rescue data and citation to previous work

claim: The lamina neurons L1 and L3 provide behaviorally relevant information to both ON and OFF pathways.
source: Taken together, these findings reveal that the lamina neurons L1 and L3 provide behaviorally relevant information to both ON and OFF pathways.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments showing contributions to both pathways

claim: L1, L2, and L3 are important inputs for both ON and the OFF pathways, relevant for visually guided behaviors across luminances.
source: In sum, our data uncover L1, L2, and L3 as important inputs for both ON and the OFF pathways, relevant for visually guided behaviors across luminances (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by comprehensive behavioral experiments

claim: Luminance information from both L1 and L3 are required for rapid luminance gain control.
source: In Drosophila, luminance information from both L1 and L3 are required for rapid luminance gain control, but the impact of the two neurons on behavior is pathway dependent.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments showing pathway-specific effects

claim: In the OFF pathway, losing either L1 or L3 function leads to a strong deviation from luminance invariance, such that the dim light stimuli are underestimated.
source: In the OFF pathway, losing either L1 or L3 function leads to a strong deviation from luminance invariance, such that the dim light stimuli are underestimated.
evidence: Supported by behavioral silencing experiments

claim: ON motion-driven behavior only underestimates dim stimuli if both L1 and L3 neuron types are not functional.
source: On the contrary, ON motion-driven behavior only underestimates dim stimuli if both L1 and L3 neuron types are not functional.
evidence: Supported by double silencing experiments

claim: L2 neurons contribute contrast-sensitive information to ON behavior.
source: Furthermore, L2 neurons, which were formerly thought to be OFF-pathway inputs, contribute contrast-sensitive information to ON behavior (Clark et al., 2011; Joesch et al., 2010; Silies et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments and citations to previous work

claim: L3 makes most synaptic connections with the Mi9 neuron that plays a role in guiding behavioral responses to ON stimuli.
source: However, L3 itself actually makes most synaptic connections with the Mi9 neuron that plays a role in guiding behavioral responses to ON stimuli (Strother et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to connectomics and functional studies

claim: Synapses of L3 with the ON-selective Mi1 neuron are similar in number to those with Tm9.
source: Further synapses of L3 with the ON-selective Mi1 neuron are similar in number to those with Tm9 (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to connectomics data

claim: L3 can potentially convey information to the chromatic pathway, as Tm20 is its second strongest postsynaptic connection.
source: Finally, L3 can potentially also convey information to the chromatic pathway, as Tm20 is its second strongest postsynaptic connection (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to connectomics data

claim: A split in ON and OFF circuitry only truly exists in downstream medulla neurons and direction-selective cells.
source: Altogether, it now becomes evident that a split in ON and OFF circuitry only truly exists in downstream medulla neurons and direction-selective cells.
evidence: Inferred from comprehensive behavioral and physiological data

claim: The luminance and contrast features encoded differently in L1, L2 and L3 lamina neurons are shared by both pathways.
source: The luminance and contrast features encoded differently in L1, L2 and L3 lamina neurons are shared by both pathways.
evidence: Supported by physiological and behavioral data

claim: L1 was previously considered the ON-pathway sibling of the contrast-sensitive L2, both with regard to its temporal filtering properties and at the transcriptome level.
source: L1 was previously considered the ON-pathway sibling of the contrast-sensitive L2, both with regard to its temporal filtering properties and at the transcriptome level (Clark et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: L1 calcium signals show a transient and a sustained response component, which are contrast- and luminance-sensitive, respectively.
source: However, L1 calcium signals show a transient and a sustained response component, which are contrast- and luminance-sensitive, respectively.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data

claim: L1 amplifies the contrast signals received from the photoreceptors, since its transient component is more pronounced than the one seen in the photoreceptor calcium traces.
source: Compared to photoreceptors, which also carry both contrast and luminance components, L1 still amplifies the contrast signals received from the photoreceptors, since its transient component is more pronounced than the one seen in the photoreceptor calcium traces (Gür et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by comparison with photoreceptor data from cited work

claim: L3's calcium responses show little adaptation and can utilize most of its operating range to encode luminance.
source: L3's calcium responses show little adaptation and can utilize most of its operating range to encode luminance.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data

claim: L3 invests its wider operating range into amplifying the darkest luminance values selectively and non-linearly.
source: L3 seems to invest this wider operating range into amplifying the darkest luminance values selectively and non-linearly.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing non-linear luminance responses

claim: A predominantly luminance-sensitive channel among LMCs may have evolved to selectively process stimuli in the low luminance range.
source: Thus, a predominantly luminance-sensitive channel among LMCs may have evolved to selectively process stimuli in the low luminance range.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of L3's non-linear luminance sensitivity

claim: The different linear and non-linear properties of L1 and L3 might further increase the dynamic range of luminance signaling.
source: The different linear and non-linear properties of L1 and L3 might further increase the dynamic range of luminance signaling (Odermatt et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation to related work

claim: In the mouse retina, more than 30 functionally distinct bipolar types show a spectrum of temporal filter properties rather than a strict transient-sustained dichotomy.
source: In the mouse retina, more than 30 functionally distinct bipolar types show a spectrum of temporal filter properties rather than a strict transient-sustained dichotomy, thus capturing a larger diversity of temporal information in parallel channels (e.g. Baden et al., 2016; Ichinose et al., 2014; Odermatt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on vertebrate retina

claim: Many bipolar cell types resemble L1, in that they have both luminance and contrast signals in distinct response components.
source: Many bipolar cell types resemble L1, in that they have both luminance and contrast signals in distinct response components (e.g. Oesch and Diamond, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on bipolar cells

claim: Some predominantly sustained bipolar cell types closely resemble the luminance-sensitive L3.
source: However, the degree of transiency varies from cell type to cell type, and some predominantly sustained bipolar cell types are also found, closely resembling the luminance-sensitive L3 (e.g. Awatramani and Slaughter, 2000; Ichinose et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on bipolar cells

claim: During daylight, visual scenes can differ in intensity by 4–5 log units, whereas electrical signals in cone photoreceptors reach a dynamic range of only two orders of magnitude.
source: For example, during daylight, visual scenes can differ in intensity by 4–5 log units, whereas electrical signals in cone photoreceptors reach a dynamic range of only two orders of magnitude (Naka and Rushton, 1966; Normann and Perlman, 1979; Pouli et al., 2010; Schnapf et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on photoreceptor physiology

claim: In insects, there are two layers of processing between photoreceptors and the first direction-selective cells: the lamina and the medulla.
source: Although the vertebrate retina apparently has a much larger diversity of cell types to handle the wide and complex statistics of the visual environments, there is only a single layer of processing between photoreceptors and the first direction-selective cells, whereas in insects, there are two: the lamina and the medulla.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of insect visual system organization

claim: The emergence of ON selectivity occurs through inhibitory glutamatergic synapses in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, the emergence of ON selectivity occurs through inhibitory glutamatergic synapses, but whereas this happens at the photoreceptor-to-bipolar cell synapse in vertebrates, it happens one synapse further down between lamina and medulla neurons in flies (Masu et al., 1995; Molina-Obando et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on ON selectivity mechanisms

claim: LMCs and downstream medulla neurons combined appear to be the functional equivalents of vertebrate bipolar cell layers.
source: Taken together, LMCs and downstream medulla neurons combined appear to be the functional equivalents of vertebrate bipolar cell layers.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of processing stages across species

claim: The photoreceptor-to-lamina synapse in the fly superposition eye serves to spatially pool information from different photoreceptors.
source: Furthermore, the photoreceptor-to-lamina synapse in the fly superposition eye already serves to spatially pool information from different photoreceptors (Braitenberg, 1967; Clandinin and Zipursky, 2002; Kirschfeld, 1967).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on fly visual system
